clinicalPearls: A disorder of midline development in which the X-linked form is caused by MID1 variants and affects males more severely
The cardinal features are hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes) and hypospadias in males
A laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft can cause swallowing difficulty, recurrent aspiration and respiratory problems in infancy
Additional midline anomalies include cleft lip and palate, imperforate anus and congenital heart defects
Developmental delay and intellectual disability are variable and often mild to moderate
Caused by variants in MID1, encoding a microtubule-associated E3 ubiquitin ligase; carrier females typically show only hypertelorism
Aspiration and airway involvement are the main early clinical threats
reference.pathophysiology: MID1 encodes a microtubule-associated protein of the TRIM/RBCC family that functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, regulating the turnover of the catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 2A and thereby influencing microtubule dynamics and signalling during midline morphogenesis. Loss-of-function variants disturb this regulation, impairing the fusion and development of ventral midline structures in the face, larynx, heart, abdomen and genitalia. The result is the constellation of hypertelorism, laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft, hypospadias and other midline defects, with variable neurodevelopmental impact. Because MID1 is X-linked, males are affected while carrier females usually show only hypertelorism.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant Opitz G/BBB syndrome (22q11.2 region)
additionalInvestigations: Swallowing assessment and airway evaluation for laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft
Renal and genital imaging and evaluation of anal anatomy
Targeted MID1 sequencing or a gene panel or exome sequencing, with chromosomal microarray to exclude 22q11.2 deletion
redFlags: Recurrent aspiration or respiratory distress from an airway or oesophageal cleft
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends largely on the severity of the laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft and cardiac anomalies; with surgical management of midline defects many children do well, though neurodevelopmental outcome is variable. Care is multidisciplinary and supportive.
pitfalls: Missing a laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft in an infant with recurrent aspiration
Not distinguishing the X-linked MID1 form from the 22q11.2-associated autosomal dominant form
Overlooking the diagnosis when only hypertelorism is present in a carrier mother
Attributing feeding problems to reflux alone without airway assessment
